hook: In 1750 a family near Manchester, England, might spin and weave wool by hand at home. By 1850 the same cloth poured out of steam-powered mills in town, run by people who had left their farms. Within a century, Britain went from a country of villages to the first country where more people lived in towns than in the countryside. What changed, and why did it start there?

prereq.q: What did the Second Agricultural Revolution do to the number of people needed on farms?
options: It lowered it, because new methods grew more food with fewer workers
It raised it, because new crops needed more hands
It moved farmworkers into cities by law
prereq.why: New tools and methods grew more food with fewer workers, freeing people to move to towns.

options: One country ruling another territory and its people
People moving from farms to cities
A country splitting into smaller states
prereq.why: Colonialism is rule over another territory; industrial powers used colonies for raw materials and markets.

prereq.q: People leaving the countryside to live in cities is called what?
prereq.why: Rural-to-urban migration is the move from the countryside to cities, a key effect of factory jobs.

figure.caption: New machines and nearby coal and iron led to factories in towns, which pulled workers to cities and sent the search for raw materials overseas.

chain.cause: New machines and the steam engine meet coal and iron in Britain
chain.effect: factories can run anywhere there is coal, so they cluster in towns

chain.cause: Factories in towns need many workers, and farms need fewer
Workers pour into towns faster than housing is built
chain.effect: cities such as Manchester grow fast and crowd up, and a working class forms

chain.cause: Mills need cotton, rubber and buyers
chain.effect: industrial countries tighten control over colonies (colonialism and imperialism)

ideas: Industrialization is the spread of factories and machine work to a place. It needs new technology and the resources to run it.
The steam engine freed factories from rivers, so they clustered in towns near coal, workers and buyers.
More food from new farm methods fed the towns and freed farmworkers, so cities grew and the population rose.
Factories needed raw materials and markets, which fed colonialism and imperialism in Africa and Asia.
Industry spread from Britain to Belgium, the Ruhr, the US Northeast and, after 1868, Japan: at different times, by different routes.

misconception.wrong: The Industrial Revolution was one quick event that happened everywhere at once.
misconception.right: It took more than a century and reached places at different times: Britain from the late 1700s, Germany's Ruhr in the mid-1800s, Japan after 1868. Name the place and the time.

summary: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the late 1700s, when new machines and steam power met coal and iron. Factories clustered in towns, farmworkers moved to cities, a working class formed, and the hunt for raw materials and markets fed colonialism.
